## Introduction

Data repositories are good.
They theoretically encourage the reuse of data.
Some groups have found very, very cool ways to reuse and reanalyze transcriptomics data, for examples.
However, as with all data, and most especially -omics level data, there are issues both with the ability to reuse the data that is there, and the data quality.
As such, we have attempted to assess the quality of a large number of datasets in an open data repository where we are very familiar with the underlying data format, the Metabolomics Workbench.

Previous related publications include

The measures we have used to assess the quality include:
  * Higher correlation with samples between subject-sample-factors;
  * P-values of subject-sample-factors and sample principal component scores;
  * The number of outlier samples detected within each subject-sample-factor;
  * The correlations of any quality-control samples, if present.

We also provide quality-control reports for a large number of analyses.

## Methods

### Detection of Log-Transformed Datasets

Some deposited abundances are already log-transformed.
We want to be able to detect them, un-transform them (exponentiate with base 2), and evaluate them in their un-transformed state.
In our experience, non-transormed dataset distributions tend to be heavily skewed with long-tailed distributions, i.e. look much like a log-normal distribution, and then the log-transformed data appears much more "normal-like".
Therefore, we can detect already log-transformed data by determining if it is "normal".
However, tests for normality are notoriously fickle and prone to return non-significant values if the data is at all different from expectations.
One common element of normally distributed data is that the mean and median of the data are relatively close together, whereas for skewed or long-tailed data the mean and median, by definition, are very different.

We calculated the mean-median-ratio (MMR) across all 5904 datasets that created a summarized experiment object, as well as the number of negative values, the maximum observed abundance, and the dynamic range (maximum / minimum values).
The dynamic range calculated in the presence of negative values involves first adding the absolute value of the minimum value, + 1, to transform all values to be positive, and subsequently calcuating the ratio of the maximum and minimum of the transformed values.

### Quality Control Cutoffs

#### Metadata Issues

Number of SSF Groups (can indicate missing sample metadata): 
  
  * N SSF > 20 ~ red;
  * 10 < N SSF < 20 ~ yellow;
  * N SSF = 1 ~ yellow;
  * N SSF < 10 ~ green


#### Number of Features and Samples

n-features:

  * n <= 9 ~ low; 
  * 10 <= n <= 29 ~ medium; 
  * n >= 30 ~ high

n-samples: 

  * n <= 3 ~ low; 
  * 3 < n < 10 ~ medium; 
  * n >= 10 ~ high

#### Number of Samples in Subject Sample Factors and Number of Subject Sample Factor Groups

Number of samples within each SSF:
  
  * all SSF have <= 2 samples ~ red;
  * 3 <= all SSF <= 4 ~ yellow;
  * all SSF >= 5 samples ~ green;
 

#### Quality Control Samples

* Has none ~ yellow;
* Has some ~ green


#### Percent Missing and Left-Censorship

* percent missing <= 2 x SD ~ green;
* 2 x SD < percent missing < 4 x SD limit ~ yellow;
* percent missing > 4 x SD limit ~ red
* percent missing > 10% & lc test p-value <= 0.05 ~ green (can we replace % missing with X number of features missing);
* percent missing > 10% & lc test p-value > 0.05 ~ yellow;

#### Maximum Observed Median RSD

* RSD <= median + 2 x SD ~ green;
* median + 2 x SD < RSD < median + 4 x SD ~ yellow;
* RSD > median + 4 x SD ~ red

#### Median Correlations

* Max Med ICI-Kt > median(Max med) - 2 SD ~ green;
* median(Max med) - 4 SD < Max Med ICI-Kt < median(Max med) - 2 SD ~ yellow;
* Max Med ICI-Kt < median(Max med) - 4 SD ~ red 

#### PCA Scores

PC that accounts for 90% of variance, we took all the values from the analyses present, log10-transformed the values, and considered only those with a log10(PC-90) >= 1.
This results in a one sided distribution that is roughly log-normal, that we can calculate the standard deviation of.
We assume a median of 1, and then calculate the standard deviation.
To get actual cutoffs, we convert the values to raw space and floor them to the nearest integer.

  * PC-90 <= median + 2 SD ~ green ; 
  * median + 2 SD < PC-90 <= median + 4 SD ~ yellow; 
  * PC-90 > median + 4 SD ~ red.

ANOVA p-adjusted: 

  * p-adjust <= 0.05 && PC-perc >= 5% ~ green; 
  * p-adjust <= 0.05 && 1% <= PC-perc < 5% ~ yellow;
  * p-adjust <= 0.05 && PC-perc < 1% ~ red;
  * p-adjusted > 0.05 ~ red.

#### Median Within vs Inter SSF ICI-Kt

SSF group size <= 5:

  * Inter better == 0 ~ green;
  * 0 < Inter better <= 1 ~ yellow;
  * Inter better > 1 ~ red;

SSF group size <= 10:

  * Inter better <= 1 ~ green;
  * 1 < Inter better <= 3 ~ yellow;
  * Inter better > 3 ~ red;

SSF group size > 10:

  * Inter better fraction <= 0.1 ~ green;
  * 0.1 < Inter better fraction <= 0.3 ~ yellow;
  * Inter better fraction > 0.3 ~ red;

  #### Number of Sample Group Sizes by Hiearchical Clustering Compared to Actual

  SSF group size <= 5:

  * size difference == 0 ~ green;
  * 0 < size difference < 2 ~ yellow;
  * size difference > 2 ~ red;

SSF group size <= 10:

  * size difference <= 1 ~ green;
  * 1 < size difference <= 4 ~ yellow;
  * size difference > 4 ~ red;

SSF group size > 10:

  * size fraction <= 0.25 ~ green;
  * size fraction > 0.25 ~ yellow;
  * size fraction > 0.5 ~ red;
